name: Password changed
description: Sent after a password is successfully changed: the change recorded with its metadata, and a way to undo it if the person who made it was not the account holder.

origin.note: Design: audit line, then alarm — no greeting, the change set as a monospaced record, and the escape hatch given a dark band of its own at the foot rather than a second button beside the first.

subject: Your {{ product.name }} password was changed
preheader: A record of the change, and what to do if it wasn't you.

heading_text.description: The headline. State the completed fact — a recipient who did not make this change needs to know that in the preview pane, not three lines in.

body.description: The opening sentence. Give the recipient permission to stop reading if it was them, so the band at the foot is aimed only at the person it is for.
body.default: The password on your account has been changed. If that was you, there is nothing to do — this message is only the record.

record_label.description: Small heading over the metadata. It is a label, not a sentence, so keep it to one or two words.

changed_at.description: When the change went through, formatted at the call site and ideally with the time zone spelled out — a bare clock time is unverifiable to someone travelling.

device.description: Browser and operating system as your session store recorded them. Recognition is the whole point, so use what the person would recognise, not the raw user agent.

ip_address.description: The address the change came from. Meaningless to most readers and decisive to the few who check it, which is why it is present but set quietly.

location.description: Approximate place derived from the address. Omit it rather than guess: a wrong city turns a reassuring email into an alarming one.

metadata_caveat.description: The honest footnote under the record. Geolocation is routinely a city or two out, and a reader who knows that will not panic at an unfamiliar name.
metadata_caveat.default: Location is estimated from the network address and is often a city or two out. Mobile networks are worse than most.

alarm_title.description: Heading of the closing band. Address the one reader it is for.

alarm_body.description: What is actually at stake and what to do about it. Say it plainly: whoever changed the password can currently read everything in the account.
alarm_body.default: Then somebody else set that password and can sign in as you right now. End every session and take the account back.

revoke_label.description: Label on the recovery action. Name both halves — signing out and resetting — because doing only one of them leaves the intruder in.

revoke_url.description: Where the account recovery flow starts. Leave it empty if your product has no self-service recovery, and point the band's copy at support instead.

closing_note.description: Why this email exists at all. Saying that it is sent on every change stops the next one being mistaken for a phishing attempt.
closing_note.default: We send this every time a password changes, including changes you make yourself from account settings. We will never ask you to reply with a password.
